questions.title: When is prior possession of a firearm considered 'intrinsic' evidence rather than Rule 404(b) other acts evidence?
questions.question_body: I'm reading *United States v. Cutbank* and the court allowed testimony that the defendant had possessed the sawed-off rifle a 'handful of times' before the charged incident. The defense argued this was propensity evidence under Rule 404(b), but the Eighth Circuit called it 'intrinsic evidence.' I'm confused about the distinction. Does 'intrinsic' just mean it's part of the same transaction, or is there a specific test for when prior possession proves continuous control? The court cited *United States v. Battle*, but I'm not sure how that applies here when the prior possession wasn't part of the specific charged offense date.

questions.title: Does USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) require a separate conviction for the 'another felony offense' enhancement?
questions.question_body: In the sentencing section, the court applied a four-level enhancement under § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) for possession 'in connection with another felony offense.' The commentary says this applies 'regardless of whether a criminal charge was brought, or a conviction obtained.' The facts mention Cutbank threatened his girlfriend and barricaded himself, which sounds like domestic assault or kidnapping, but I don't see a conviction for those specific acts in the opinion. How can the court enhance the sentence based on a 'felony offense' if he wasn't charged or convicted of that underlying felony? What is the burden of proof for that underlying conduct at sentencing?

questions.title: How does the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) interact with USSG § 4B1.4(b) when calculating the Guidelines range?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that the jury found Cutbank had three prior violent felonies, triggering ACCA penalties. However, the PSR calculated a base offense level under § 2K2.1 resulting in a level of 35, while the 'Armed Career Criminal Guideline' (§ 4B1.4) would have produced level 34. The court says 'The Guidelines provide that the greater offense level applies.' I thought ACCA imposed a mandatory statutory minimum of 15 years. How does the Guidelines calculation interact with the ACCA statutory minimum? Does the Guidelines level determine the starting point for the statutory range, or are they separate calculations that just happen to overlap?

questions.title: When is a limiting instruction required for hearsay statements when the declarant testifies at trial?
questions.question_body: Cutbank requested a limiting instruction regarding D.F.'s statements to the police before she testified, arguing hearsay and Confrontation Clause issues. The district court refused to give an instruction at the time the evidence was admitted, relying on the fact that D.F. later testified in person. The Eighth Circuit affirmed, citing *United States v. Bennett*. I thought the Confrontation Clause (Crawford) might still require specific handling of pre-trial statements even if the witness testifies. Under what circumstances is the declarant's testimony sufficient to cure the need for a limiting instruction on their prior hearsay statements?

questions.title: To what extent can emotionally prejudicial background information be admitted during impeachment regarding prior inconsistent statements?
questions.question_body: During cross-examination, D.F. testified that she didn't remember seeing the gun because her sister was killed by a gun. The defense moved to strike this under Rule 403 as prejudicial, but the court denied it. The opinion says this testimony 'responded to cross-examination regarding inconsistent prior statements.' I'm struggling to understand the Rule 403 balancing here. If the probative value is just to explain a prior inconsistency, does that outweigh the high risk of unfair prejudice regarding a family member's death? Is there a specific exception for impeachment credibility that relaxes Rule 403?

questions.title: What is the standard of review for a within-Guidelines sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)?
questions.question_body: The court affirms the sentence because it was within the advisory guidelines range and cites a 'presumption of reasonableness' from *United States v. Goodhouse*. Cutbank argued the sentence was substantively unreasonable under § 3553(a). I'm confused about the procedural posture here. If the sentence is within the range, does the appellate court only look for procedural error, or do they still review substantive reasonableness? Also, the opinion mentions the district court didn't provide a 'mechanical recitation' of factors. What is the minimum record requirement to show the district court actually considered the § 3553(a) factors?
